claim: Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) are the dominant framework for modeling response time (RT) data from speeded decision-making tasks.
source: Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) are the dominant framework for modeling response time (RT) data from speeded decision-making tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the field's consensus on modeling approaches.

claim: EAMs do not explain how the visual system extracts perceptual representations in the first place.
source: While providing a good quantitative description of RT data in terms of abstract perceptual representations, EAMs do not explain how the visual system extracts these representations in the first place.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of existing EAM models.

claim: The visual accumulator model (VAM) integrates convolutional neural network models of visual processing with traditional EAMs.
source: To address this limitation, we introduce the visual accumulator model (VAM), in which convolutional neural network models of visual processing and traditional EAMs are jointly fitted to trial-level RTs and raw (pixel-space) visual stimuli from individual subjects in a unified Bayesian framework.
evidence: This describes the core architecture of the proposed model.

claim: VAMs fitted to large-scale cognitive training data from a stylized flanker task captured individual differences in congruency effects, RTs, and accuracy.
source: Models fitted to large-scale cognitive training data from a stylized flanker task captured individual differences in congruency effects, RTs, and accuracy.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model fitting results.

claim: The selection of task-relevant information occurs through the orthogonalization of relevant and irrelevant representations.
source: We find evidence that the selection of task-relevant information occurs through the orthogonalization of relevant and irrelevant representations, demonstrating how our framework can be used to relate visual representations to behavioral outputs.
evidence: This is a key mechanistic finding from the representation geometry analyses.

claim: The diffusion-decision model is an example of an evidence accumulation model.
source: Evidence accumulation models (EAMs), such as the diffusion-decision model (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Ratcliff, 1978) and linear ballistic accumulator model (LBA) (Brown and Heathcote, 2008), are the most successful and widely-used computational models of joint RT and choice data from decision-making tasks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the relevant literature.

claim: The linear ballistic accumulator model (LBA) is an example of an evidence accumulation model.
source: Evidence accumulation models (EAMs), such as the diffusion-decision model (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Ratcliff, 1978) and linear ballistic accumulator model (LBA) (Brown and Heathcote, 2008), are the most successful and widely-used computational models of joint RT and choice data from decision-making tasks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the relevant literature.

claim: In the EAM framework, sensory evidence is accumulated until reaching a threshold, at which point an overt response is generated.
source: In the EAM framework, sensory evidence is accumulated (possibly with noise) until reaching a threshold, at which point an overt response is generated.
evidence: This describes the core mechanism of EAMs based on established literature.

claim: EAMs have been shown to capture RT distributions from a variety of cognitive tasks at the individual subject level.
source: Empirically, EAMs have been shown to capture RT distributions from a variety of cognitive tasks at the individual subject level (Brown and Heathcote, 2008; Ratcliff, 1978; Usher and McClelland, 2001; Ratcliff and Rouder, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: EAMs do not typically provide a detailed specification of how raw visual stimuli are transformed into evidence in visual tasks.
source: In the context of visual tasks, EAMs do not typically provide a detailed specification of how raw visual stimuli are transformed into evidence and consequently do not explain the visual processing steps underlying decision-making.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of EAMs in the context of visual tasks.

claim: Recent modeling efforts have adapted CNN models to generate RTs or RT proxies.
source: A number of recent modeling efforts have addressed this limitation by adapting convolutional neural network (CNN) models used in image classification tasks to the novel purpose of generating RTs or RT proxies (Spoerer et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2021; Kumbhar et al., 2020; Rafiei et al., 2024; Goetschalckx et al., 2023; Annis et al., 2021; Holmes et al., 2020; Trueblood et al., 2021), a strategy we also pursue here.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent work.

claim: CNNs are image-computable, meaning they accept arbitrary images as input.
source: CNNs are useful in this regard since they are image-computable—they accept arbitrary images as input—and capture important characteristics of biological vision (Lindsay, 2021; Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Kriegeskorte, 2015).
evidence: This is a known property of CNNs.

claim: CNNs capture important characteristics of biological vision.
source: CNNs are useful in this regard since they are image-computable—they accept arbitrary images as input—and capture important characteristics of biological vision (Lindsay, 2021; Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Kriegeskorte, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the neuroscience literature.

claim: Early CNN layers exhibit spatially-organized units with local receptive fields, analogous to the retinotopic organization of the early mammalian visual pathway.
source: Early CNN layers exhibit spatially-organized units with local receptive fields, analogous to the retinotopic organization of the early mammalian visual pathway.
evidence: This is a known correspondence between CNNs and biological vision.

claim: The concatenation of multiple CNN layers forms a hierarchy in which progressively more abstract features are extracted in deeper layers.
source: The concatenation of multiple layers forms a hierarchy in which progressively more abstract features are extracted in deeper layers, in a way that is globally similar to the primate visual cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This describes a known property of CNNs and their similarity to biological vision.

claim: The VAM accepts raw (pixel-space) visual stimuli as inputs and generates RTs and choices as outputs.
source: As in the prior models referenced above, the VAM accepts raw (pixel-space) visual stimuli as inputs and generates RTs and choices as outputs.
evidence: This describes the input-output structure of the VAM.

claim: In the VAM, the CNN and EAM parameters are jointly fitted to the RT, choice, and visual stimulus data from individual participants in a unified Bayesian framework.
source: The key feature of the VAM that distinguishes it from prior models is that the CNN and EAM parameters are jointly fitted to the RT, choice, and visual stimulus data from individual participants in a unified Bayesian framework.
evidence: This describes the key methodological innovation of the VAM.

claim: In the VAM, both the visual representations learned by the CNN and the EAM parameters are directly constrained by behavioral data.
source: Thus, both the visual representations learned by the CNN and the EAM parameters are directly constrained by behavioral data.
evidence: This is a consequence of the joint fitting approach.

claim: Prior models first optimize the CNN to perform the behavioral task, then separately fit CNN parameters and/or EAM parameters to behavioral data.
source: In contrast, prior models first optimize the CNN to perform the behavioral task, then separately fit a minimal set of high-level CNN parameters (Rafiei et al., 2024) and/or the EAM parameters to behavioral data (Annis et al., 2021; Holmes et al., 2020; Trueblood et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the approach taken by prior models, supported by citations.

claim: Fitting the CNN with human data has significant consequences for the representations learned by the model.
source: As we will show, fitting the CNN with human data—rather than optimizing the model to perform a task—has significant consequences for the representations learned by the model.
evidence: This is a key finding that will be demonstrated in the results.

claim: Deep neural network models of vision optimized to perform particular tasks do not account for many results from psychology.
source: In doing so, our framework also addresses one of the main criticisms of deep neural network models of vision that are optimized to perform particular tasks (e.g. object identification): these models do not account for many results from psychology (Baker et al., 2018; Bowers et al., 2022; Fel et al., 2022; Lindsay, 2021; Malhotra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Lost in Migration (LIM) is a stylized version of the arrows flanker task.
source: LIM is a stylized version of the well-known arrows flanker task used in the study of cognitive control and visual attention (Figure 1A; Stoffels and van der Molen, 1988).
evidence: This describes the task used in the study, with reference to Figure 1A and a citation.

claim: In LIM, participants indicate the direction of the central bird (the target) using arrow keys, ignoring the surrounding birds (the flankers).
source: In LIM, participants are shown stimuli composed of several arrow-shaped birds. The task is to indicate the direction of the central bird (the target) using the arrow keys on the keyboard, ignoring the direction of the surrounding birds (the flankers).
evidence: This describes the task instructions.

claim: Participants engage with LIM at home and are rewarded via a composite score that takes into account both speed and accuracy.
source: Participants engage with the task at home and are rewarded via a composite score that takes into account both speed and accuracy.
evidence: This describes the task context and reward structure.

claim: In LIM, both targets and flankers can be independently oriented left, right, up, or down.
source: First, both targets and flankers can be independently oriented left, right, up, or down, such that there are four possible response directions (the standard arrow flanker task allows for only left and right responses).
evidence: This describes a feature of the LIM task that differs from the standard flanker task.

claim: The layout of targets and flankers in LIM can appear in one of seven configurations: left/right/up/down 'V,' horizontal/vertical line, and cross.
source: Second, the layout of the targets and the flankers can appear in one of seven configurations: left/right/up/down 'V,' horizontal/vertical line, and cross (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the stimulus layouts, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In LIM, the target can be centered anywhere within the 640×480 pixel game window, subject to edge constraints.
source: Last, the target can be centered anywhere within the 640×480 pixel game window, subject to edge constraints.
evidence: This describes the spatial variability of stimuli in LIM.

claim: A trial is congruent if targets and flankers are oriented in the same direction, and incongruent otherwise.
source: As with other flanker tasks, a given trial is said to be congruent if targets and flankers are oriented in the same direction, and incongruent otherwise.
evidence: This defines the congruency condition used in flanker tasks.

claim: Participants are slower and less accurate on incongruent trials in flanker tasks.
source: A consistent observation from studies employing the flanker task and related conflict tasks are congruency effects: participants are slower and less accurate on incongruent trials (Eriksen and Eriksen, 1974; Simon, 1982; Stroop, 1935).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Congruency effects index the extent to which an individual can selectively attend to task-relevant information and ignore irrelevant information.
source: Congruency effects are considered to index a specific aspect of cognitive control: they indicate the extent to which an individual can selectively attend to task-relevant information and ignore irrelevant information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of congruency effects based on cognitive control theory.

claim: The visual accumulator is composed of a CNN and EAM chained together.
source: The visual accumulator is an image-computable EAM, composed of a CNN and EAM chained together (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the architecture of the VAM, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Minimally processed (pixel-space) visual stimuli are provided as inputs to the CNN in the VAM.
source: Minimally processed (pixel-space) visual stimuli are provided as inputs to the CNN.
evidence: This describes the input to the VAM.

claim: The outputs of the CNN correspond to the mean rates at which evidence is accumulated (the drift rates).
source: The outputs of the CNN correspond to the mean rates at which evidence is accumulated (the drift rates), one for each possible response (four in the case of LIM).
evidence: This describes how the CNN outputs are used in the EAM.

claim: The EAM generates choices and RTs through a noisy evidence accumulation process.
source: The EAM then generates choices and RTs through a noisy evidence accumulation process.
evidence: This describes the function of the EAM component.

claim: For each participant in the dataset, one VAM (CNN + EAM) was fitted jointly using that participant's visual stimuli, RTs, and choices.
source: For each participant in the dataset, we fit one such model (CNN + EAM) jointly using that participant's visual stimuli, RTs, and choices.
evidence: This describes the model fitting procedure.

claim: An automatic differentiation variational inference (ADVI) algorithm was developed to simultaneously optimize the CNN parameters and learn the posterior distribution over the LBA parameters.
source: Building on prior work (Dao et al., 2024; Kucukelbir et al., 2017), we developed an automatic differentiation variational inference (ADVI) algorithm that simultaneously optimizes the parameters of the CNN and learns the posterior distribution over the LBA parameters (Methods).
evidence: This describes the inference algorithm used, with citations to prior work.

claim: The LBA was adopted as the EAM because it can be applied to tasks with more than two possible responses.
source: The particular EAM we adopt is the linear ballistic accumulator model (LBA Brown and Heathcote, 2008; Figure 1B) since it can be applied to tasks with more than two possible responses, though the general VAM framework is compatible with other EAMs that have a closed-form or easily approximated likelihood.
evidence: This explains the choice of the LBA model, with a citation.

claim: A seven layer CNN architecture (six convolutional layers, one fully-connected layer) was used in the VAM.
source: We used a seven layer CNN architecture (six convolutional layers, one fully-connected layer) in the VAM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the CNN architecture, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The first two convolutional layers of the VAM CNN were initialized with parameters from a 16-layer VGG CNN trained to classify the ImageNet dataset.
source: To speed up the training process, the first two convolutional layers were initialized with the parameters from a 16-layer VGG CNN trained to classify the ImageNet dataset (Deng et al., 2009; Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015).
evidence: This describes the initialization procedure, with citations.

claim: A separate VAM was fitted to LIM data from each of 75 Lumosity users.
source: We fitted a separate VAM to LIM data (visual stimuli, RTs, choices) from each of 75 Lumosity users (participants).
evidence: This describes the sample size and modeling approach.

claim: Participants were selected who had practiced Lost in Migration extensively (≥25,000 trials).
source: We selected participants who had practiced Lost in Migration extensively (≥25,000 trials) and used data from a later stage of practice to minimize learning effects (≥ each participant's 50th gameplay).
evidence: This describes the participant selection criteria.

claim: Participants varied in age (23–87 y) and in their behavior (mean RT, accuracy, congruency effects).
source: These participants varied in age (23–87 y) and in their behavior (mean RT, accuracy, congruency effects), allowing us to examine how well our framework captured individual differences.
evidence: This describes the variability in the participant sample.

claim: The responses of the fitted models were highly correlated with those of the participants for mean RT, accuracy, RT congruency effect, and accuracy congruency effect (Pearson's r > 0.75).
source: For each behavioral summary statistic, the responses of the fitted models were highly correlated with those of the participants (Pearson's r > 0.75), with slopes close to unity (Figure 2B–E, statistics in figure legend).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The RT congruency effect could be attributed to a reduction in the mean target drift rate parameter on incongruent vs. congruent trials.
source: We found that the RT congruency effect could be attributed to a reduction in the mean target drift rate parameter on incongruent vs. congruent trials, while the accuracy congruency effect could be attributed to a higher mean flanker drift rate on incongruent trials relative to the non-target (other) mean drift rates on congruent trials (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model parameters, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: The accuracy congruency effect could be attributed to a higher mean flanker drift rate on incongruent trials relative to the non-target (other) mean drift rates on congruent trials.
source: We found that the RT congruency effect could be attributed to a reduction in the mean target drift rate parameter on incongruent vs. congruent trials, while the accuracy congruency effect could be attributed to a higher mean flanker drift rate on incongruent trials relative to the non-target (other) mean drift rates on congruent trials (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model parameters, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Mean RTs began increasing around age 50 in both participants and fitted models.
source: Mean RTs began increasing around age 50, effects captured by the fitted models (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: An age-dependent reduction in the target drift rates was observed in the models.
source: We also observed an age-dependent reduction in the target drift rates and no age-dependence of the flanker drift rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), findings that have received mixed support in the literature (Ben-David et al., 2014; Forstmann et al., 2011; Ratcliff, 1978; Servant and Evans, 2020; Steyvers et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: No age-dependence of the flanker drift rates was observed in the models.
source: We also observed an age-dependent reduction in the target drift rates and no age-dependence of the flanker drift rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), findings that have received mixed support in the literature (Ben-David et al., 2014; Forstmann et al., 2011; Ratcliff, 1978; Servant and Evans, 2020; Steyvers et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: The majority of participants exhibited layout-dependent RT biases (p<0.05 for 60/75 participants).
source: The majority of participants exhibited layout-dependent RT biases (p<0.05 for 60/75 participants, one-way ANOVA; see examples in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The median Pearson's r between model/participant mean RTs across each layout was 0.67 for participants with significant layout-dependent RT modulation.
source: We quantified how well the models captured these effects by calculating the Pearson's r between model/participant mean RTs across each layout for the participants that exhibited significant layout-dependent RT modulation (Figure 2J). The median Pearson's r was 0.67, demonstrating good correspondence between model/participant behavior.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation, with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: Responses to trials with the vertical line layout were on average somewhat faster than the other layouts for both participants and models.
source: There was considerable heterogeneity in the particular layout RT biases exhibited by both the participants and models, though responses to trials with the vertical line layout were on average somewhat faster than the other layouts for both participants and models (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, with reference to figures.

claim: The majority of participants exhibited both horizontal and vertical position-dependent RT biases (horizontal: p<0.05 for 72/75 participants, vertical: p<0.05 for 69/75 participants).
source: The majority of participants also exhibited both horizontal and vertical position-dependent RT biases (horizontal position: p<0.05 for 72/75 participants, vertical position: p<0.05 for 69/75 participants, one-way ANOVA; see examples in Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The median Pearson's r between model/participant mean RTs across stimulus position bins was 0.78 for horizontal position and 0.55 for vertical position.
source: The fitted models captured these effects adequately: the median Pearson's r between model/participant mean RTs across stimulus position bins was 0.78 for horizontal position and 0.55 for vertical position (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation, with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: Most participants/models responded more slowly when the stimuli were positioned close to the horizontal edges and vertical edges of the task window.
source: While there was substantial variability across both participants and models in the particular position-dependent RT biases they exhibited, most participants/models responded more slowly when the stimuli were positioned close to the horizontal edges and, to a lesser extent, the vertical edges of the task window (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, with reference to figures.

claim: The participant RT delta plots showed that the congruency effect increased with longer RTs.
source: The participant RT delta plots showed that the congruency effect increased with longer RTs (Pratte, 2021), a trend that was captured by the fitted VAMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, with a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The fitted VAMs captured the trend that the congruency effect increased with longer RTs.
source: The participant RT delta plots showed that the congruency effect increased with longer RTs (Pratte, 2021), a trend that was captured by the fitted VAMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the model evaluation, with reference to a figure.

claim: A mismatch was observed between model and participant behavior for the conditional accuracy functions on incongruent trials.
source: In contrast, we observed a mismatch between model and participant behavior for the conditional accuracy functions on incongruent trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the model evaluation, with reference to a figure.

claim: Participants tended to be less accurate on faster trials, while the models exhibited the opposite trend.
source: In particular, the participants tended to be less accurate on faster trials, while the models exhibited the opposite trend.
evidence: This is an observation from the conditional accuracy function analysis.

claim: The lack of dynamic visual processing in the VAM may explain the discrepancy in conditional accuracy functions.
source: This discrepancy may be explained by the lack of dynamic visual processing in the VAM, which has been proposed to account for the preponderance of errors on faster trials often observed in conflict tasks (White et al., 2011; van den Wildenberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed discrepancy, with citations.

claim: Decoding performance on holdout data for target direction was near chance (27%) in the first network layer.
source: Decoding performance on holdout data for target direction was near chance (27%) in the first network layer and increased to nearly perfect decoding (≥ 97%) at layer 4, with a sharp increase between the second and third convolutional layers (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the decoding analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Decoding performance for target direction increased to nearly perfect (≥ 97%) at layer 4.
source: Decoding performance on holdout data for target direction was near chance (27%) in the first network layer and increased to nearly perfect decoding (≥ 97%) at layer 4, with a sharp increase between the second and third convolutional layers (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the decoding analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: There was a sharp increase in target direction decoding accuracy between the second and third convolutional layers.
source: Decoding performance on holdout data for target direction was near chance (27%) in the first network layer and increased to nearly perfect decoding (≥ 97%) at layer 4, with a sharp increase between the second and third convolutional layers (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the decoding analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The increase in target decoding accuracy from shallower to deeper network layers is consistent with neural recording studies and other neural network studies.
source: The increase in target decoding accuracy from shallower to deeper network layers is generally consistent with neural recording studies in mammals and other neural networks studies that document more accurate decoding of abstract variables (e.g. object or category identity) in higher visual/cortical regions and deeper neural network layers (Brincat et al., 2018; Muratore et al., 2022; Tafazoli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Information for target direction exhibited a non-monotonic 'hunchback' profile across the convolutional layers at the single-unit level.
source: In contrast to the population-level decoding results, information for target direction exhibited a non-monotonic 'hunchback' profile across the convolutional layers, then increased sharply in the final fully-connected layer.
evidence: This is a result from the single-unit information analysis.

claim: Single-unit information for target direction increased sharply in the final fully-connected layer.
source: In contrast to the population-level decoding results, information for target direction exhibited a non-monotonic 'hunchback' profile across the convolutional layers, then increased sharply in the final fully-connected layer.
evidence: This is a result from the single-unit information analysis.

claim: The decrease in single-unit information for target direction between the fourth and final convolutional layers indicates that units become progressively less selective for particular target directions.
source: The observation that single-unit information for target direction decreased between the fourth and final convolutional layers indicates that the units become progressively less selective for particular target directions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the single-unit information results.

claim: The decrease in single-unit selectivity combined with high population-level decoding suggests a transition to a more distributed, ensemble-level code.
source: Since population-level decoding remained high in these layers, this suggests a transition from representing target direction with specialized 'target neurons' to a more distributed, ensemble-level code.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined single-unit and population-level results.

claim: A similar transition in coding properties takes place along the cortical hierarchy, with higher-order cortical regions exhibiting a reduction in units with 'pure' selectivity and an increase in units with mixed selectivity.
source: Notably, a similar transition in coding properties takes place along the cortical hierarchy, with higher-order cortical regions exhibiting a reduction in units with 'pure' selectivity and a corresponding increase in units with mixed selectivity for multiple task or stimulus features (Annis et al., 2021; Meister et al., 2013; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to neuroscience findings, supported by citations.

claim: The high proportion of units with mixed selectivity results in a high-dimensional representation in which all task-relevant information can easily be extracted with simple linear decoders.
source: The high proportion of units with mixed selectivity results in a high-dimensional representation in which all task-relevant information can easily be extracted with simple linear decoders (Cover, 1965; Pagan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about high-dimensional representations, supported by citations.

claim: The dimensionality of target representations increased sharply in the last two convolutional layers (Conv5–Conv6).
source: Consistent with these ideas, we found that the dimensionality of target representations as measured by the participation ratio (Methods) increased sharply in the last two convolutional layers (Conv5–Conv6), paralleling the reduction in single-unit information for target direction in these layers (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality analysis, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The high-dimensional representation in Conv5-Conv6 may enable the VAM to capture the rich stimulus-behavior dependencies present in the participant data.
source: The high-dimensional representation observed in these layers may enable the VAM to capture the rich stimulus-behavior dependencies present in the participant data.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the high dimensionality.

claim: The reduction in dimensionality in the final fully-connected layer may reflect a strong constraint to select the correct target direction imposed by the task.
source: The reduction in dimensionality in the final fully-connected layer, and concomitant increase in single-unit information for target direction, may reflect a strong constraint to select the correct target direction imposed by the task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the dimensionality reduction.

claim: The hunchback-shaped profile observed in the dimensionality of representations has also been observed along visual cortical regions of the rat ventral stream and in other neural network studies.
source: Notably, the hunchback-shaped profile we observed in the dimensionality of representations has also been observed along visual cortical regions of the rat ventral stream and in other neural network studies (Ansuini et al., 2019; Muratore et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The proportion of units that were selective for a particular direction increased steadily from the second to the fourth convolutional layer.
source: The proportion of units that were selective for a particular direction increased steadily from the second to the fourth convolutional layer, with most units exhibiting positive modulation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the selectivity analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Between the fourth and final convolutional layers, the proportion of units with positive target direction modulation decreased, while the proportion of units with negative and complex modulation increased.
source: Between the fourth and final convolutional layers, the proportion of units with positive target direction modulation decreased, while the proportion of units with negative and complex modulation increased.
evidence: This is a result from the selectivity analysis.

claim: Generalization performance for target direction in different distracter contexts was initially near chance (25%) and increased steadily through the network layers.
source: For each type of distracting information, we found that generalization performance was initially near chance (25%) and increased steadily through the network layers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the tolerance analysis, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The lower generalization performance for flanker direction in the deepest network layers (∼60%) can be attributed to the robust congruency effects exhibited by the models.
source: The lower generalization performance for flanker direction observed in the deepest network layers (∼60%) can be attributed to the robust congruency effects exhibited by the models (Figure 2D, E): for the vast majority of incongruent error trials, the model chose the flanker direction, implying that flanker direction has a strong impact on model representations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the generalization results, with reference to figures.

claim: Decoding accuracy for flanker direction and stimulus layout exhibited a hunchback profile in which decoding performance started low in early layers, increased in intermediate layers, and decreased in later layers.
source: We found that decoding accuracy for flanker direction and stimulus layout exhibited a hunchback profile in which decoding performance started low in early layers, increased in intermediate layers, and decreased in later layers (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the decoding analysis, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The decoding accuracy for horizontal and vertical position showed a steady increase until the second-to-last layer, followed by a slight drop in the last layer.
source: The decoding accuracy for horizontal and vertical position followed a similar but shifted pattern: there was a steady increase in accuracy until the second-to-last layer, followed by a slight drop in the last layer.
evidence: This is a result from the decoding analysis.

claim: Partial suppression of irrelevant stimulus features is expected given that these features all impact behavior.
source: Partial (rather than complete) suppression of irrelevant stimulus features is expected given that these features all impact behavior (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the suppression results, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Information for the irrelevant stimulus features exhibited a pronounced hunchback profile in the progression from shallower to deeper network layers at the single-unit level.
source: In agreement with the population-level decoding analyses, information for the irrelevant stimulus features exhibited a pronounced hunchback profile in the progression from shallower to deeper network layers.
evidence: This is a result from the single-unit information analysis.

claim: The suppression of irrelevant information is more pronounced at the single-unit level than at the population level.
source: It is noteworthy that the suppression of irrelevant information is more pronounced at the single-unit level in that decoding accuracy remains relatively high in later layers, particularly for flanker direction.
evidence: This is a comparison of single-unit and population-level results.

claim: No significant positive correlation was observed between flanker direction decoding accuracy or mutual information and RT or accuracy congruency effects in most layers.
source: However, we did not observe a significant positive correlation between either decoding accuracy or mutual information and RT or accuracy congruency effects in any of the model layers, with the exception of a single significant positive correlation between flanker mutual information and accuracy congruency effects in layer Conv3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Target and flanker subspaces are well-aligned beginning at the third convolutional layer.
source: Beginning at the third convolutional layer, when decoding accuracy for both targets and flankers is high (>90%), we found that target and flanker subspaces are well-aligned.
evidence: This is a result from the subspace alignment analysis.

claim: The high alignment of target and flanker subspaces in the third convolutional layer is evidence that the model has learned a common representation for direction that is shared for both targets and flankers.
source: We interpret the high alignment as evidence that the model has learned a common representation for direction that is shared for both targets and flankers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the subspace alignment results.

claim: In later layers, target and flanker representations become increasingly orthogonal.
source: In later layers, we found that target and flanker representations become increasingly orthogonal, consistent with the view that the processing in later layers acts to reduce interference between task-relevant and irrelevant information.
evidence: This is a result from the subspace alignment analysis.

claim: A significant positive correlation was observed between subspace alignment and accuracy congruency effects across models in each layer beginning with the fourth convolutional layer.
source: Consistent with this idea, we observed a significant positive correlation between subspace alignment and accuracy congruency effects across models in each layer beginning with the fourth convolutional layer (Figure 5B andC; adjusted p-value<0.05 for layers 3–7, permutation test, Bonferroni correction for seven comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: No significant correlation was observed between target/flanker subspace alignment and RT congruency effects in any network layer.
source: In contrast, we did not observe a significant correlation between target/flanker subspace alignment and RT congruency effects in any network layer, suggesting a mechanistic dissociation between RT and accuracy congruency effects (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The task-optimized models did not exhibit an accuracy congruency effect.
source: We found that the task-optimized models did not exhibit an accuracy congruency effect (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of task-optimized models and VAMs, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Simply training the model to perform the task is not sufficient to reproduce the accuracy congruency effect.
source: Thus, simply training the model to perform the task is not sufficient to reproduce a behavioral phenomenon widely-observed in conflict tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task-optimized model results.

claim: The task-optimized models had lower target/flanker subspace alignment (higher orthogonalization) for all network layers beginning with the third convolutional layer.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that the task-optimized models had lower target/flanker subspace alignment (i.e. higher orthogonalization) for all network layers beginning with the third convolutional layer (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of task-optimized models and VAMs, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The dimensionality of the VAM and task-optimized model representations was nearly identical for the first four convolutional layers.
source: We found that the dimensionality of the VAM and task-optimized model representations was nearly identical for the first four convolutional layers (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality comparison, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: For the final two convolutional layers, the VAMs exhibited a substantially more pronounced expansion of dimensionality than the task-optimized models.
source: In contrast, for the final two convolutional layers, the VAMs exhibited a substantially more pronounced expansion of dimensionality than the task-optimized models.
evidence: This is a result from the dimensionality comparison.

claim: Relative to the VAMs, the task-optimized models had substantially higher single-unit information for both target and flanker direction in layers Conv5–Conv6.
source: Relative to the VAMs, the task-optimized models had substantially higher single-unit information for both target and flanker direction in layers Conv5–Conv6 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a result from the single-unit information comparison, with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Population-level decoding accuracy for target/flanker direction and stimulus position was similar between the task-optimized models and VAMs in layers Conv5–Conv6.
source: In contrast, population-level decoding accuracy for target/flanker direction and stimulus position was similar between the task-optimized models and VAMs in layers Conv5–Conv6, though decoding accuracy for stimulus layout was notably lower for the task-optimized models (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the decoding comparison, with reference to figures.

claim: The task-optimized models maintained a simpler code for target/flanker direction in the later convolutional layers relative to the VAMs.
source: These results suggest that the task-optimized models maintained a simpler code for target/flanker direction in the later convolutional layers relative to the VAMs, primarily relying on separate populations of directionally-tuned units.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between task-optimized models and VAMs.

claim: The task-optimized models had a higher proportion of simple selective (+) directionally-tuned units and a lower proportion of complex units in layers Conv5–6 relative to the VAMs.
source: Consistent with this idea, the task-optimized models had a higher proportion of simple selective (+) directionally-tuned units and a lower proportion of complex units in layers Conv5–6 relative to the VAMs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a result from the selectivity comparison, with reference to Figure 6F.
